blind_reading.passage: Mark 1:5 / Matthew 3:5-6 (John the Baptist at the Jordan)
blind_reading.what_triggered_it: Crowds coming down to a river to be baptized in water by an unnamed 'servant of God' is essentially the John-the-Baptist scene with the name swapped out.

constraints.finding: 'πολλοὶ κατέβαινον πρὸς τὸν ποταμόν, καὶ ὁ δοῦλος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐβάπτιζεν αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ὕδατι' reconstructs the unmistakable Synoptic baptism-at-the-Jordan scene (crowds descending to a river, being baptized by a designated agent in water) even though no verbatim string is copied and John is not named.

echo.finding: The two-clause structure (crowd movement toward the river + agent baptizing them in water) mirrors the Gospel baptism reports closely.
The scene — many people going down to a river to be baptized by a designated 'servant of God' — is the John the Baptist episode in all but name.
'ἐβάπτιζεν αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ὕδατι' collocates baptizer, recipients, and water in the same configuration as the Gospel baptism formula (ἐβαπτίζοντο ... ἐν τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ / ἐν ὕδατι).
'ὁ δοῦλος τοῦ θεοῦ' functions as a substitute title for John the Baptist, importing a quasi-canonical role rather than a neutral illustrative agent.

reasoning_audit.finding: The reasoning claims the sentence anchors the rite 'without borrowing a Gospel line,' but this only checks for verbatim wording, not scene identity. The generator never asks whether the constructed scene itself is recognizable as the Baptist narrative — it is, and the swap test for the verb does not address this concern at all.

βαπτίζω.summary: The sentence, while grammatically sound and correctly targeting ἐβάπτιζεν, reconstructs the John-the-Baptist-at-the-Jordan scene (crowds descending to a river to be baptized by a designated servant of God in water); the generator should relocate the action away from a river/crowd/agent triad that mirrors Mark 1:5 while keeping the same target form.

blind_reading.passage: Mark 10:46-52 / Luke 18:35-43 (blind Bartimaeus/blind beggar crying out by the road)
blind_reading.what_triggered_it: τυφλὸς ... ἔκραξεν μεγάλῃ φωνῇ amid a crowd is the exact shape of the blind man's cry that the crowd tries to suppress in the healing-of-the-blind-man stories.

constraints.finding: διὰ τὸν θόρυβον τοῦ ὄχλου (διά + accusative) is causal ('because of/on account of the uproar'), not concessive. The sentence as written literally says the disciples heard him *because of* the crowd's noise, which is nonsensical given the intended sense.
Translation 'despite the uproar of the crowd' does not match the causal διά + accusative construction actually written; it silently converts a causal clause into a concessive one.

echo.finding: τυφλὸς ... ἔκραξεν is the pivotal wording of the Bartimaeus pericope, though not a verbatim run.
The two-clause shape (blind man cries out — reaction of bystanders to the noise) mirrors the Gospel scene's structure of crowd-vs-cry.

A blind man shouting loudly while surrounded by a noisy crowd, with someone else's hearing/response depending on that noise, is precisely the healing-narrative scene, only with 'disciples hearing him' substituted for 'Jesus/crowd rebuking him'.
ὁ τυφλός + ἔκραξεν is a recognizable collocation from this narrative, even though μεγάλῃ φωνῇ is generic elsewhere in the NT.

reasoning_audit.finding: The reasoning claims 'the concessive ὅτι-free structure with ἀλλά shuts out the reading spoke,' but the actual sentence uses καί, not ἀλλά — there is no adversative conjunction in the card at all. The reasoning describes a sentence that was not written. It also asserts a concessive sense for διὰ τὸν θόρυβον that the Greek does not support (διά + accusative is causal), so the stated disambiguation logic doesn't correspond to the actual grammar of the sentence.

κράζω.summary: Fix the mismatch between reasoning and text (there is no ἀλλά, only καί) and correct the mistranslated διὰ τὸν θόρυβον (causal 'because of', not concessive 'despite'), and consider softening the scene so it doesn't so closely retrace the blind-man-crying-out-amid-the-crowd episode from Mark 10/Luke 18.

blind_reading.what_triggered_it: Rulers persecuting believers over their faith and the believers fleeing a city closely mirrors the pattern of civic/authority-driven persecution and nighttime escape found in Acts.

constraints.finding: The translation 'they fled' assigns ἔφυγον to τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς, but Greek narrative convention keeps the subject of a coordinated verb the same as the preceding clause absent a marked shift (δέ, or a new subject noun). As written, οἱ ἄρχοντες remains the most natural subject of ἔφυγον, so the Greek more plausibly says 'the rulers fled the city' — the opposite of the intended scene.
Same ambiguity as above: the sentence does not unambiguously encode which party flees, undermining the very persecution-plus-flight scenario the card is built to teach.

echo.finding: Two coordinated finite clauses with no subject-marking device (δέ, οἱ δὲ ἀδελφοί) closely follows a common Acts narrative pattern of persecution-then-flight, but here it backfires: the same structure that recalls Acts also makes the subject of the second verb default to the first clause's subject.
The intended scene (brothers flee persecution) is not the scene the syntax most naturally delivers (rulers flee).

reasoning_audit.finding: The reasoning asserts 'believers fleeing a city while rulers drive them out gives hostility plus motion' as if this were unambiguously encoded in the Greek, but the reasoning never checks who ἔφυγον's subject actually is. It describes the intended scene, not the scene the sentence's syntax delivers by default (continuous subject = οἱ ἄρχοντες).

διώκω.summary: Fix the dangling subject of ἔφυγον — add an explicit subject (e.g. οἱ δὲ ἀδελφοὶ ἔφυγον) so the brothers, not the rulers, are unambiguously the ones fleeing; the διώκω usage and tense pairing are otherwise fine and can stay.

blind_reading.what_triggered_it: A woman with a great fever (πυρετὸν μέγαν / πυρετῷ μεγάλῳ) who is healed and rises (ἠγέρθη) is the exact shape of the Capernaum fever-healing scene.

constraints.finding: The sentence reconstructs a recognizable Gospel episode (fever, healing, rising) rather than a neutral invented scene, risking the item being learned as a scripture paraphrase rather than a plain vocabulary sentence.

echo.finding: πυρετὸν μέγαν closely mirrors συνεχομένη πυρετῷ μεγάλῳ.
The three-beat sequence (fever → healed → rose) matches the healing-and-rising pattern almost beat for beat.
Woman, great fever, healing, rising from the bed is the specific Capernaum scene, not a generic illness scenario.
πυρετός + μέγας is an uncommon pairing outside this narrative, making its reuse here conspicuous.

reasoning_audit.finding: The reasoning justifies θεραπεύω's sense (recovery from named ailment, resulting change of state) correctly, but it never addresses that the illustrative scene it built to make that sense 'visible' is the well-known fever-healing narrative from Mark/Luke. It defends the lexical choice while ignoring that the vehicle for demonstrating it is a recognizable Gospel scene, which is the actual risk in this card.

θεραπεύω.summary: The target word and gloss are handled correctly, but the sentence reconstructs the healing of Peter's mother-in-law (great fever, healing, rising from bed) almost scene-for-scene; the generator should keep θεραπεύω but change the ailment/scene so it no longer echoes Mark 1:29-31 / Luke 4:38-39.

blind_reading.passage: Luke 13:25 (cf. Mark's 'ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης' formula, e.g. Mark 1:32, 4:35, 6:47)
blind_reading.what_triggered_it: The scene of a stranger knocking outside a shut door while the οἰκοδεσπότης controls opening it closely mirrors Luke 13:25's 'ἐγερθῇ ὁ οἰκοδεσπότης καὶ ἀποκλείσῃ τὴν θύραν... ἔξω ἑστάναι καὶ κρούειν τὴν θύραν', and the opening genitive absolute 'ὀψίας γενομένης' echoes Mark's recurring temporal formula.

constraints.finding: The sentence reconstructs the core scene of Luke 13:25 (householder shutting a door, someone left knocking ἔξω, the householder as the one who opens/shuts) almost point for point, and opens with the Markan formulaic genitive absolute 'ὀψίας γενομένης'. This is more than incidental vocabulary overlap — it is a recognizable allusion, which the no-echo constraint is meant to rule out.

echo.finding: 'ἔξω ἔκρουεν' directly parallels Luke 13:25's 'ἔξω ἑστάναι καὶ κρούειν τὴν θύραν'.
The opening genitive absolute 'ὀψίας γενομένης' reproduces a recurring Markan narrative formula almost verbatim.
A shut door, a person locked outside knocking, and the οἰκοδεσπότης as the one who opens/shuts is the exact scene of Luke 13:25, not a generic invented one.
θύρα + κρούω + ἔξω + οἰκοδεσπότης co-occur in the source text as they do here.

reasoning_audit.finding: The reasoning only defends the sense-disambiguation choice (physical door vs. 'opportunity') and never considers whether the scene itself is original. It misses that the combination of shut door, knocking outside, and the οἰκοδεσπότης opening/shutting is a near-verbatim recall of Luke 13:25, and that 'ὀψίας γενομένης' is a stock Markan phrase — the argument addresses a different, easier question than the one the card actually raises.

θύρα.summary: The sentence's scene and vocabulary (shut door, knocking ἔξω, οἰκοδεσπότης opening it, opening with 'ὀψίας γενομένης') reconstructs Luke 13:25 and Markan formulaic phrasing rather than an original context; the generator should invent a scene for θύρα that does not reuse this collocation of door + knocking + householder.
